London Air Quality Analysis (2017–2024)¶

Trends, weather drivers, the COVID-19 lockdown, and predicting pollution levels¶

Author: Cristina · Data: London Air Quality Network (Imperial College London) + Open-Meteo ERA5 reanalysis

1. Project objectives¶

This project answers four questions about air pollution in London:

  1. Trends – How have NO₂, PM₂.₅ and O₃ levels changed between 2017 and 2024?
  2. Patterns & drivers – How do pollutants vary by season, day of week and hour, and which weather factors matter most?
  3. COVID-19 lockdown – Did the spring 2020 lockdown (less traffic) measurably improve air quality, once we account for the weather?
  4. Prediction – Can we forecast tomorrow's average pollution level from today's data and the weather?

SMART targets
Specific Daily mean NO₂ and PM₂.₅ at North Kensington (urban background)
Measurable Beat a persistence baseline ("tomorrow = today") on RMSE on a held-out year (2024)
Achievable Public hourly data, standard Python libraries (pandas, scikit-learn)
Relevant NO₂ and PM₂.₅ are the main pollutants behind London's health burden and policies like ULEZ
Time-bound Week 1 data collection & cleaning · Week 2 EDA · Week 3 lockdown analysis · Week 4 modelling & write-up

Monitoring sites¶

Code Site Type Why it is interesting
MY1 Westminster – Marylebone Road Kerbside One of the busiest roads in London; strong traffic signal
KC1 Kensington & Chelsea – North Kensington Urban background Long, complete record of all three pollutants
BL0 Camden – Bloomsbury Urban background Central London background (data ends 2023)

All concentrations are in µg/m³.

2. Data collection¶

  • Air quality: hourly measurements from the London Air Quality Network (LAQN) API, run by Imperial College London's Environmental Research Group.
  • Weather: hourly ERA5 reanalysis for central London from the Open-Meteo historical weather API: temperature, humidity, rain, wind, pressure, cloud, solar radiation and boundary-layer height (how deep the "mixing lid" over the city is).

The CSVs in data_raw/ were downloaded on 16 Nov 2026. The functions below can rebuild them from scratch (set REFETCH = True). This takes a few minutes because the LAQN API is slow.

In [2]:
REFETCH = False

def fetch_laqn(site, species, start_year=2017, end_year=2024):
    """Download hourly data for one LAQN site/species, quarter by quarter."""
    import requests
    rows = []
    for y in range(start_year, end_year + 1):
        for a, b in [("01-01", "04-01"), ("04-01", "07-01"), ("07-01", "10-01"), ("10-01", "01-01")]:
            end = f"{y + 1 if b == '01-01' else y}-{b}"
            url = (f"https://api.erg.ic.ac.uk/AirQuality/Data/SiteSpecies/SiteCode={site}"
                   f"/SpeciesCode={species}/StartDate={y}-{a}/EndDate={end}/Json")
            data = requests.get(url, timeout=120).json()["RawAQData"].get("Data", [])
            rows += [(d["@MeasurementDateGMT"], d["@Value"]) for d in data]
    s = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["time_gmt", f"{site}_{species}"]).replace("", np.nan)
    s["time_gmt"] = pd.to_datetime(s["time_gmt"])
    return s.drop_duplicates("time_gmt").set_index("time_gmt").astype(float)

def fetch_weather(lat=51.52, lon=-0.15, start="2017-01-01", end="2024-12-31"):
    import requests
    hourly = ("temperature_2m,relative_humidity_2m,precipitation,wind_speed_10m,wind_direction_10m,"
              "surface_pressure,cloud_cover,shortwave_radiation,boundary_layer_height")
    url = (f"https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive?latitude={lat}&longitude={lon}"
           f"&start_date={start}&end_date={end}&hourly={hourly}&timezone=GMT&models=era5")
    h = requests.get(url, timeout=120).json()["hourly"]
    return pd.DataFrame(h).rename(columns={"time": "time_gmt"})

if REFETCH:
    pairs = [("MY1", "NO2"), ("MY1", "O3"), ("KC1", "NO2"), ("KC1", "PM25"), ("KC1", "O3"),
             ("BL0", "NO2"), ("BL0", "PM25"), ("BL0", "O3")]
    aq_new = pd.concat([fetch_laqn(s, p) for s, p in pairs], axis=1)
    aq_new.to_csv(DATA_DIR / "london_aq_hourly_2017_2024.csv")
    fetch_weather().to_csv(DATA_DIR / "london_weather_hourly_2017_2024.csv", index=False)

3. Data cleaning¶

Steps:

  1. Regular hourly index. Put both tables on the same complete hourly timeline (GMT), so gaps show up as NaN instead of missing rows.
  2. Negative values. Monitors report small negative readings near zero (instrument noise). Values down to −5 µg/m³ are set to 0. Anything lower would be treated as invalid (there are none).
  3. Completeness check. Measure data capture per site and year. The usual rule for annual statistics is ≥ 75 % capture, so site-years below that are flagged and left out of the trend charts.
  4. Merge with weather and add calendar features (local London time, so "rush hour" means rush hour).

What the data looks like after cleaning

  • North Kensington (KC1) has the most complete record: NO₂ and O₃ are above 85 % every year. PM₂.₅ coverage drops in 2023–24, with a long gap in spring 2024.
  • Marylebone Road (MY1) has no PM₂.₅ data in this period, so it is used for NO₂ and O₃ only.
  • Bloomsbury (BL0) stops reporting in mid-2023, and its PM₂.₅ is patchy from 2021.
  • Negative values were rare (largest −4 µg/m³) and were set to 0.
In [6]:
# Merge + calendar features (local time for human-activity patterns)
df = aq.join(wx)
local = df.index.tz_localize("UTC").tz_convert("Europe/London")
df["hour"] = local.hour
df["dow"] = local.dayofweek            # 0 = Monday
df["month"] = local.month
df["year"] = df.index.year
df["is_weekend"] = (df["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)
# Wind as vector components (360° and 0° are the same direction)
rad = np.deg2rad(df["wind_direction_10m"])
df["wind_u"] = -df["wind_speed_10m"] * np.sin(rad)   # +ve = blowing towards east (from the west)
df["wind_v"] = -df["wind_speed_10m"] * np.cos(rad)   # +ve = blowing towards north (from the south)

# Boundary-layer height (BLH) is missing for Jan–Jun 2024 in the ERA5 archive.
# Fill it with a model that predicts BLH from the other weather variables, trained on all other hours.
blh_feats = ["temperature_2m", "relative_humidity_2m", "precipitation", "wind_speed_10m", "wind_u", "wind_v",
             "surface_pressure", "cloud_cover", "shortwave_radiation", "hour", "month"]
known = df["boundary_layer_height"].notna()
print("Missing BLH hours:", (~known).sum(), "→", df.index[~known].min().date(), "to", df.index[~known].max().date())
blh_train = df.loc[known & (df.index < "2023-01-01")]
blh_check = df.loc[known & (df.index >= "2023-01-01")]
blh_model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(blh_train[blh_feats], blh_train["boundary_layer_height"])
print(f"BLH gap-filling model, R² on held-out 2023–24 hours: {r2_score(blh_check['boundary_layer_height'], blh_model.predict(blh_check[blh_feats])):.2f}")
blh_model.fit(df.loc[known, blh_feats], df.loc[known, "boundary_layer_height"])
df["blh_imputed"] = (~known).astype(int)
df.loc[~known, "boundary_layer_height"] = blh_model.predict(df.loc[~known, blh_feats])

df.to_csv("london_air_quality_clean.csv")   # saved so later notebooks/apps can start from clean data
print(df.shape)
df.describe().T[["count", "mean", "std", "min", "50%", "max"]]

4. Exploratory data analysis¶

4.1 Long-term trend¶

For reference:

  • UK legal limit (annual mean): NO₂ 40 µg/m³, PM₂.₅ 20 µg/m³ (England's 2040 target: 10 µg/m³)
  • WHO 2021 guideline (annual mean): NO₂ 10 µg/m³, PM₂.₅ 5 µg/m³

Findings: trends

  • NO₂ has roughly halved at both kerbside and background sites since 2017 (−50 % at Marylebone Road, −51 % at North Kensington by 2023).
  • At Marylebone Road the annual mean was more than double the UK legal limit (40 µg/m³) in 2017–18, met the limit for the first time in 2024 (32.5), and recorded zero hours above the 200 µg/m³ hourly limit from 2019 onwards (39 hours in 2017).
  • PM₂.₅ fell about 40 % at North Kensington (11.6 → 7.0 µg/m³). That is well within the UK limit and close to England's 2040 target of 10, but still above the WHO guideline of 5.
  • Ozone went up (+32 % at N. Kensington, +82 % at Marylebone Road). This is expected: NO emitted by traffic destroys O₃ locally ("NOx titration"). With less traffic NOx, less ozone is used up, so cutting NO₂ partly trades off against O₃.

The steepest fall at Marylebone Road comes right after the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) launched in central London in April 2019. The kerbside monthly mean dropped from about 80 to about 60 µg/m³ within months, before COVID. The lockdown then produced a temporary dip, followed by a slower decline through the ULEZ expansions in 2021 and 2023. This chart shows timing only and does not prove cause: fleet renewal and other policies were happening at the same time.

# Weekday vs weekend daily profile: the "traffic fingerprint"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, s in zip(axes, ["MY1", "KC1"]):
    prof = pre.groupby(["is_weekend", "hour"])[f"{s}_NO2"].mean().unstack(0)
    ax.plot(prof.index, prof[0], lw=2.5, color=SITE_COLORS[s], label="Weekday")
    ax.plot(prof.index, prof[1], lw=2.5, color=SITE_COLORS[s], ls="--", alpha=0.7, label="Weekend")
    ax.set_title(f"NO₂ – {SITE_NAMES[s]}"); ax.set_xlabel("Hour (local)"); ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 3))
    ax.legend()
axes[0].set_ylabel("µg/m³")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "05_weekday_weekend.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

Findings: cycles

  • Seasonal: NO₂ and PM₂.₅ peak in winter, when the air near the ground is shallow and still and there is more heating. O₃ peaks in spring and early summer, when sunlight drives the photochemistry.
  • Weekly: NO₂ is about 20–25 % lower on Sundays than on weekdays. PM₂.₅ barely changes through the week, which points to sources beyond local traffic. O₃ is highest at weekends (less NO to destroy it).
  • Daily: at the background site NO₂ has a clear morning rush-hour peak (7–9 am) on weekdays that disappears at weekends, and an evening build-up as the boundary layer collapses after sunset. O₃ mirrors NO₂ and peaks mid-afternoon.
  • At Marylebone Road weekday NO₂ stays high all day and peaks around 4–5 pm at about 105 µg/m³ (2017–19). That is the traffic fingerprint of a congested arterial road.

Findings: weather

  • Boundary-layer height has the strongest link to background NO₂ and PM₂.₅ (ρ ≈ −0.6). Since mid-2021, North Kensington NO₂ averages about 31 µg/m³ when the mixing layer is shallow (< 200 m) and about 6 when it is deep (> 1.2 km). The same emissions are simply diluted into more or less air.
  • Wind speed works the same way: calm conditions (< 8 km/h) bring more than three times the NO₂ compared with strong winds (> 24 km/h).
  • Wind direction tells you where pollution comes from. NO₂ at North Kensington is fairly uniform, consistent with local sources all around. PM₂.₅ is highest with easterly winds, which bring polluted continental air (secondary particles from European agriculture and industry). Much of London's PM₂.₅ is not made in London.
  • Street canyon: Marylebone Road runs east–west and the monitor stands on the south side. With winds from the north its NO₂ is about half what it is with southerly or westerly winds. The vortex that forms inside the canyon carries exhaust onto whichever side is upwind. Because of this, the hourly model for MY1 below relies heavily on the north–south wind component.
  • Daily correlations at Marylebone Road look weak only because its long-term decline (−50 %) is larger than day-to-day weather effects. The model in section 6 separates the two.

5. Did the 2020 lockdown clean London's air?¶

England's first national lockdown began on 23 March 2020. Traffic in London dropped sharply. Simply comparing spring 2020 with spring 2019 is misleading for two reasons:

  • Weather differs from year to year (spring 2020 was unusually sunny and dry).
  • Policy trend: NO₂ was already falling (for example, ULEZ launched in April 2019).

This section first runs the naive comparison, then a weather-normalised ("business-as-usual") counterfactual: a model trained on pre-lockdown data predicts what pollution would have been in spring 2020 under the actual weather, and that prediction is compared with what was measured.

In [16]:
LOCK_START, LOCK_END = "2020-03-23", "2020-05-12"   # strictest phase (before the first easing on 13 May)
def window(df_, year):
    return df_.loc[f"{year}-03-23":f"{year}-05-12"]

series = ["MY1_NO2", "KC1_NO2", "BL0_NO2", "KC1_PM25", "KC1_O3"]
naive = pd.DataFrame({
    "2017–19 same dates": pd.concat([window(df, y)[series] for y in [2017, 2018, 2019]]).mean(),
    "2020 lockdown": window(df, 2020)[series].mean(),
})
naive["change %"] = (naive["2020 lockdown"] / naive["2017–19 same dates"] - 1) * 100
naive.round(1)

# Weather-normalised counterfactual (business as usual)
features_bau = ["temperature_2m", "relative_humidity_2m", "precipitation", "wind_speed_10m", "wind_u", "wind_v",
                "surface_pressure", "cloud_cover", "shortwave_radiation", "boundary_layer_height",
                "hour", "dow", "month", "trend"]
df["trend"] = (df.index - df.index[0]).days   # lets the model learn the slow pre-2020 decline

TRAIN_END = "2020-03-15"   # pre-lockdown training data (people started staying home ~16 March)
results, bau_preds = {}, {}
for target in series:
    train = df.loc[:TRAIN_END, features_bau + [target]].dropna()
    model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=400, learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=31,
                                          random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    model.fit(train[features_bau], train[target])
    period = df.loc["2020-02-01":"2020-07-31", features_bau + [target]].dropna(subset=features_bau)
    period["bau"] = model.predict(period[features_bau])
    bau_preds[target] = period[[target, "bau"]]
    lock = period.loc[LOCK_START:LOCK_END].dropna()
    results[target] = {
        "observed": lock[target].mean(),
        "business-as-usual": lock["bau"].mean(),
        "lockdown effect (µg/m³)": lock[target].mean() - lock["bau"].mean(),
        "lockdown effect (%)": (lock[target].mean() / lock["bau"].mean() - 1) * 100,
    }
lock_effect = pd.DataFrame(results).T
lock_effect.round(1)

Can the business-as-usual model be trusted? Before the lockdown its fit looks almost perfect, but that is in-sample. As an honest check, the same model is retrained on data up to 31 Dec 2019 and asked to predict 1 Jan – 15 Mar 2020, which it has never seen and which was still "normal". If it can predict normal weeks well, the gap during lockdown can be attributed to the lockdown rather than to model error.

In [18]:
check = {}
for target in series:
    tr = df.loc[:"2019-12-31", features_bau + [target]].dropna()
    te = df.loc["2020-01-01":"2020-03-15", features_bau + [target]].dropna()
    m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=400, learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=31, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(tr[features_bau], tr[target])
    p = m.predict(te[features_bau])
    te_d = pd.DataFrame({"obs": te[target], "pred": p}).resample("D").mean().dropna()
    check[target] = {"R² (daily)": r2_score(te_d["obs"], te_d["pred"]),
                     "mean bias (%)": (p.mean() / te[target].mean() - 1) * 100}
pd.DataFrame(check).T.round(2)

Reading the validation: the NO₂ and O₃ business-as-usual models track normal weeks well at the background sites (daily R² ≈ 0.7–0.9). They slightly under-predict normal levels (bias −6 % to −17 %), so the NO₂ reductions estimated above are, if anything, conservative. At Marylebone Road the day-to-day fit is weak (R² ≈ 0.1) because the site was still falling fast after ULEZ, so its number should be read as approximate. For PM₂.₅ the model fails on early 2020 (R² < 0, +80 % bias): Jan–Mar 2020 was exceptionally stormy and clean, and PM₂.₅ depends mostly on regional and continental air masses that local weather variables do not capture. The PM₂.₅ lockdown estimate is therefore not reliable.

Findings: lockdown

  • After accounting for the weather, the strict lockdown phase cut NO₂ by about 46 % at Marylebone Road and about 32–33 % at the two background sites. That is roughly 28 µg/m³ at the kerbside and 9–13 µg/m³ in the background. The naive comparison (−58 % at Marylebone Road) overstates the kerbside effect because it also counts the pre-existing ULEZ decline.
  • O₃ went up by about 25 % above business-as-usual. Less NO from traffic meant less ozone destroyed, helped along by the unusually sunny spring.
  • PM₂.₅ did not fall. The naive change is only −8 %, and the business-as-usual model cannot be trusted for PM₂.₅ (see the validation above). This matches published studies: London's PM₂.₅ is dominated by regional and secondary sources, and spring 2020 had several imported pollution episodes.
  • Takeaway: removing most traffic gives a large, immediate cut in NO₂ but little or no PM₂.₅ benefit on its own. Traffic policy (like ULEZ) is the right tool for NO₂, while PM₂.₅ needs regional and international action plus attention to domestic burning.

6. What drives pollution? (explanatory model)¶

An hourly gradient-boosting model is fitted using only weather and calendar features (no past pollution values), trained on Jul 2021 – Dec 2023 and tested on 2024. Permutation importance then shows which factors the model relies on most: how much the R² drops when one feature is randomly shuffled.

In [21]:
features_x = ["temperature_2m", "relative_humidity_2m", "precipitation", "wind_speed_10m", "wind_u", "wind_v",
              "surface_pressure", "cloud_cover", "shortwave_radiation", "boundary_layer_height",
              "hour", "dow", "month"]
nice = {"temperature_2m": "Temperature", "relative_humidity_2m": "Humidity", "precipitation": "Rain",
        "wind_speed_10m": "Wind speed", "wind_u": "Wind E–W component", "wind_v": "Wind N–S component",
        "surface_pressure": "Air pressure", "cloud_cover": "Cloud cover", "shortwave_radiation": "Solar radiation",
        "boundary_layer_height": "Boundary-layer height", "hour": "Hour of day", "dow": "Day of week",
        "month": "Month", "trend": "Long-term trend"}

imp_all, r2_x = {}, {}
for target in ["MY1_NO2", "KC1_NO2", "KC1_PM25", "KC1_O3"]:
    d = df[features_x + [target]].dropna()
    # train on the post-ULEZ, post-COVID period so that the level is comparable; test on 2024
    tr, te = d.loc["2021-07-19":"2023-12-31"], d.loc["2024-01-01":]
    m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=400, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(tr[features_x], tr[target])
    r2_x[target] = r2_score(te[target], m.predict(te[features_x]))
    sample = te.sample(min(len(te), 6000), random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    pi = permutation_importance(m, sample[features_x], sample[target], n_repeats=5, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, scoring="r2")
    imp_all[target] = pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=features_x)
imp = pd.DataFrame(imp_all).rename(index=nice)
print("Out-of-sample R² (2024) from weather + calendar only:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in r2_x.items()})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 4.8), sharey=True)
order = imp.mean(axis=1).sort_values().index
for ax, col in zip(axes, imp.columns):
    ax.barh(order, imp.loc[order, col], color=SITE_COLORS[col[:3]] if "NO2" in col else ("#8e44ad" if "PM25" in col else "#16a085"))
    ax.set_title(f"{POLL_NAMES[col.split('_')[1]]} – {col[:3]}"); ax.set_xlabel("Drop in R² when shuffled")
fig.suptitle("Which factors matter? (permutation importance, test set 2024)", fontweight="bold", y=1.02)

Out-of-sample R² (2024) from weather + calendar only: {'MY1_NO2': 0.26, 'KC1_NO2': 0.63, 'KC1_PM25': 0.16, 'KC1_O3': 0.65}

Findings: drivers

  • NO₂ (background): boundary-layer height dominates, followed by hour of day (the traffic cycle) and temperature. In other words: emissions × how much air they mix into.
  • NO₂ (Marylebone Rd): the north–south wind component and hour of day dominate, which is the street-canyon effect plus traffic patterns.
  • PM₂.₅: boundary-layer height, then season, temperature and the east–west wind component (continental imports). Weather and calendar alone explain little of hourly PM₂.₅ (R² ≈ 0.16), which again shows that much of it comes from far away.
  • O₃: humidity, temperature, boundary-layer height and month, the ingredients of sunny, photochemically active weather.

7. Predicting tomorrow's pollution¶

Task: predict tomorrow's daily mean NO₂ and PM₂.₅ at North Kensington, using:

  • pollution today and in recent days (lags 1, 2 and 7 days, and a 7-day rolling mean),
  • tomorrow's weather (in practice this would come from a weather forecast; here observed weather stands in for a perfect forecast),
  • calendar features (day of week, month).

Time-based split (no shuffling, so the model never sees the future): train 2017–2022 · validate 2023 · test 2024.

Models compared

  1. Persistence baseline: tomorrow = today
  2. Climatology baseline: the average for that calendar month in the training years
  3. Linear regression
  4. Random forest
  5. Gradient boosting (HistGradientBoosting)
In [22]:
def make_daily_features(df_, target):
    d = df_.resample("D").mean(numeric_only=True)
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=d.index)
    out["y"] = d[target]
    out["lag1"] = d[target].shift(1)
    out["lag2"] = d[target].shift(2)
    out["lag7"] = d[target].shift(7)
    out["roll7"] = d[target].shift(1).rolling(7, min_periods=5).mean()
    for c in ["temperature_2m", "relative_humidity_2m", "precipitation", "wind_speed_10m", "wind_u", "wind_v",
              "surface_pressure", "cloud_cover", "shortwave_radiation", "boundary_layer_height"]:
        out[c] = d[c]
    out["wind_speed_change"] = d["wind_speed_10m"] - d["wind_speed_10m"].shift(1)
    out["dow"] = out.index.dayofweek
    out["is_weekend"] = (out["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)
    out["month"] = out.index.month
    out["doy_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * out.index.dayofyear / 365.25)
    out["doy_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * out.index.dayofyear / 365.25)
    # exclude the COVID-disrupted period (Mar 2020 – Jun 2021) from training: not representative
    out["covid"] = ((out.index >= "2020-03-16") & (out.index < "2021-07-19")).astype(int)
    return out.dropna()

def evaluate(y, yhat):
    return {"RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y, yhat)), "MAE": mean_absolute_error(y, yhat), "R²": r2_score(y, yhat)}

model_results, test_preds, fitted = {}, {}, {}
for target in ["KC1_NO2", "KC1_PM25"]:
    data = make_daily_features(df, target)
    feats = [c for c in data.columns if c not in ("y", "covid")]
    train = data.loc[:"2022-12-31"].query("covid == 0")
    val = data.loc["2023-01-01":"2023-12-31"]
    test = data.loc["2024-01-01":"2024-12-31"]
    clim = train.groupby("month")["y"].mean()

    models = {
        "Linear regression": LinearRegression(),
        "Random forest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=400, min_samples_leaf=3, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "Gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.04, max_leaf_nodes=15,
                                                           l2_regularization=1.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    }
    rows, preds = {}, {"Observed": test["y"], "Persistence": test["lag1"]}
    for split_name, split in [("Validation 2023", val), ("Test 2024", test)]:
        rows[("Persistence", split_name)] = evaluate(split["y"], split["lag1"])
        rows[("Climatology", split_name)] = evaluate(split["y"], split["month"].map(clim))
    for name, m in models.items():
        m.fit(train[feats], train["y"])
        for split_name, split in [("Validation 2023", val), ("Test 2024", test)]:
            rows[(name, split_name)] = evaluate(split["y"], m.predict(split[feats]))
        preds[name] = pd.Series(m.predict(test[feats]), index=test.index)
    model_results[target] = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
    test_preds[target] = pd.DataFrame(preds)
    fitted[target] = (models, feats, test)

for target, res in model_results.items():
    print(f"\n=== {POLL_NAMES[target.split('_')[1]]} at North Kensington: daily mean, next-day forecast ===")
    display(res.unstack(1).round(2))

    models, feats, test = fitted[target]
    m = models["Gradient boosting"]
    pi = permutation_importance(m, test[feats], test["y"], n_repeats=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, scoring="r2")
    s = pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=[nice.get(f, f) for f in feats]).sort_values().tail(10)
    ax.barh(s.index, s.values, color="#8e44ad" if "PM25" in target else SITE_COLORS["KC1"])
    ax.set_title(f"{POLL_NAMES[target.split('_')[1]]} forecast: top-10 features"); ax.set_xlabel("Drop in R² when shuffled")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "13_forecast_importance.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

Findings: forecasting

  • Both pollutants beat the persistence baseline on the unseen 2024 test year, so the SMART target is met.
    • NO₂: gradient boosting RMSE 5.4 µg/m³ vs 7.8 for persistence (−30 %), R² = 0.61.
    • PM₂.₅: random forest / gradient boosting RMSE 3.1 µg/m³ vs 3.75 for persistence (−17 to −18 %), R² ≈ 0.5.
  • Climatology performs worst, especially for NO₂ (R² < 0). Monthly averages from 2017–22 are simply too high for 2024 because levels have fallen so much. Models need recent observations (lags) to stay calibrated in a changing city.
  • The forecast depends on today's level plus tomorrow's boundary-layer height and wind change, the same physics found in the EDA. For PM₂.₅ the east–west wind (continental imports) and air pressure (stagnant high-pressure episodes) matter too.
  • Linear regression is a respectable runner-up, and tree models are best but only modestly better. With roughly 1,600 training days, more complex models would add little. Remaining errors are concentrated on episode days (e.g. the November 2024 PM₂.₅ spike), which are the days that matter most for health alerts.

Limitations

  • Observed weather was used as a stand-in for a forecast. A real system would use forecast weather and would perform somewhat worse.
  • Only three monitoring sites were used. PM₂.₅ data has gaps in 2023–24, and boundary-layer height for Jan–Jun 2024 was gap-filled with a model (R² = 0.89).
  • The lockdown counterfactual assumes the pre-2020 relationship between weather and pollution held during spring 2020. The validation check shows this is reasonable for NO₂ and O₃ but not for PM₂.₅.

8. Conclusions¶

Question Answer
How has air quality changed? NO₂ halved 2017→2023 at kerbside and background sites. Marylebone Road went from 2× the legal limit to compliance (2024) and no longer has hourly exceedances. PM₂.₅ fell ~40 % but remains above WHO guidance. O₃ rose as NOx fell.
What drives daily pollution? Mostly atmospheric mixing (boundary-layer height, wind speed) on top of the traffic cycle. Wind direction matters too: easterly winds import PM₂.₅ from the continent, and the Marylebone Road street canyon halves readings in northerly winds.
Did lockdown help? Yes for NO₂: −46 % kerbside, −32 % background after removing weather effects. No clear improvement for PM₂.₅, and ozone rose by about a quarter.
Can we predict it? Next-day daily means are predictable with R² ≈ 0.5–0.6, beating persistence by 17–30 %. Recent levels and the mixing forecast are the key inputs.

Implications for policy: traffic measures such as ULEZ are very effective against NO₂, and the lockdown showed how much of kerbside NO₂ comes from traffic. PM₂.₅ is a regional problem: the lockdown removed most traffic and PM₂.₅ barely moved, so it needs action on domestic wood burning, agriculture (ammonia) and cross-border pollution.

Possible extensions¶

  1. Add more sites (outer London, ULEZ boundary) for a difference-in-differences evaluation of the 2021 and 2023 ULEZ expansions.
  2. Use real weather forecasts (e.g. Open-Meteo's historical forecast API) to make the prediction task fully realistic.
  3. Predict the probability of a high-pollution day (classification) to support health alerts.
  4. Link to health data (e.g. asthma admissions from the OHID Fingertips API) for the health-impact angle mentioned in the original project plan.
